overview: The fallout from President Trump's push to return Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive dominated the news: Huang apologized to staff, lawmakers in both parties renewed calls for limits on chip sales to China, and Monday's stock rally faded on Tuesday. Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran man whose mistaken deportation became a test case for the administration's immigration crackdown, left the U.S. voluntarily for Spain, the Department of Homeland Security said. The Army planned to detonate about five tons of deteriorating lead azide at its Iowa ammunition plant on Wednesday morning, despite objections from nearby residents. Abroad, Yemen's Houthis struck a financial tower in Riyadh again and claimed an attack on a Saudi refinery.

stories.headline: Huang apologizes to Nvidia staff as Trump's role in his return draws scrutiny
stories.summary: Jensen Huang told Nvidia employees at an all-hands meeting on Tuesday that he is in therapy and apologized for his past conduct, a day after the board reinstated him as CEO. President Trump, who pressed for Huang's return, said a pardon for him is "always an option" but probably won't be needed. Huang is due to testify before Congress next week, and lawmakers in both parties are pushing new limits on chip sales to China.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is one of the largest stocks in most retirement and index funds, so its leadership turmoil reaches ordinary 401(k)s. The case also tests how far a president can go in steering a private company in which he holds shares.
stories.background: Huang co-founded Nvidia, whose chips power much of the AI industry, and ran it for more than three decades. Earlier this month he resigned as CEO after reports of extramarital affairs, one reportedly with a woman suspected of spying for China, and the board opened an independent investigation and named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO. Trump, who has a close relationship with Huang, publicly pushed for his return, and the board reinstated him this week. Financial disclosures show Trump owns tens of millions of dollars in Nvidia stock.

facts.text: Huang told Nvidia staff on Tuesday that he is in therapy, apologized for his conduct and said it was not acceptable that he had broken a code of conduct he helped write.
Huang dismissed suggestions that he returned because Trump pressured Nvidia's board, according to Reuters' account of the meeting.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang thanked the Trump administration while addressing staff.
Nvidia's board reinstated Huang after pressure from Trump, CNBC and the Washington Examiner reported.
Trump holds tens of millions of dollars in Nvidia shares, according to financial disclosure documents reviewed by CBS News.
Trump said a pardon for Huang is "always an option" but likely won't be necessary, and that Huang should not need to invoke the Fifth Amendment before Congress.
Huang is scheduled to testify on Capitol Hill next week, and Trump's statement that Huang is not a national security threat drew criticism from members of both parties.
Lawmakers in both chambers are pushing to add new restrictions on AI chip sales to China to the year-end defense bill, The Hill reported.
Nvidia's board is facing criticism over how it handled the crisis.
Huang resigned as CEO in mid-November after reports of extramarital affairs, and the board named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO and opened an independent investigation.

stories.headline: Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves the U.S. for Spain
stories.summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran man the Trump administration wrongly deported to El Salvador last year, left the United States for Spain on Tuesday, the Department of Homeland Security said. Sen. Chris Van Hollen confirmed the departure and said he will be safe. The move ends a legal fight of about 20 months.
stories.why_it_matters: His case became the best-known test of whether courts can make the government undo a deportation it admits was a mistake, and it shaped the wider debate over due process in the administration's deportation push.
stories.background: Abrego Garcia, who lived in Maryland, was deported in March 2025 to a prison in El Salvador despite a 2019 court order barring his removal there, which the government later called an administrative error. After the Supreme Court said the government must help bring him back, he was returned in June 2025 to face federal human-smuggling charges in Tennessee, which he denied. A federal judge in Maryland ordered him released from immigration detention in December 2025. More recently, The New York Times reported, he faced the prospect of being deported to Liberia.

stories.headline: Army sets Wednesday detonation of lead explosives in Iowa after court declines to block it
stories.summary: The Army planned to detonate about 5 tons of degraded lead azide, the nation's entire stockpile, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday morning, after a federal appeals court on Monday declined to stop it. Army officials say the material could explode on its own and that precautions will limit lead dust. Residents of Iowa, Illinois and Missouri have raised health concerns about the plume.
stories.why_it_matters: Lead is harmful even in small amounts, especially for children, so people downwind are being asked to follow shelter guidance on a holiday travel day. The case also shows how the government handles aging hazardous munitions near towns.
stories.background: Lead azide is a sensitive explosive used in military detonators. The Army stored 68 drums of it underground at the Middletown plant near Burlington, Iowa, and a safety review this year found it had become unstable as crystals formed. The EPA issued an emergency permit on Nov. 13 allowing the blast, and environmental groups asked a federal appeals court to halt it. State and local leaders asked for delays, and the date shifted several times before the Army settled on Wednesday.

facts.text: The Army planned to detonate 68 drums, about 5 tons, of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday morning.
The material is the entire U.S. stockpile of lead azide.
A federal appeals court on Monday declined to block the detonation.

Federal officials said they scheduled the blast for Wednesday, ahead of evening snow, because cold temperatures could create more unstable crystals; the acting Army secretary called the plan better than a "worst-case scenario."
The Army said it has taken precautions and there is no reason to panic.
Forecast maps showed the lead dust plume area stretching from near Burlington, Iowa, toward Macon, Missouri, by noon Wednesday, subject to weather changes.
Middletown residents were told to shelter in place, and some residents said shifting guidance left them confused about where the dust would go.
The EPA issued an emergency permit for the detonation on Nov. 13, and environmental groups asked the 8th Circuit to halt it.
A safety review in March found the stored lead azide had become unstable.

stories.headline: Democrats reach at least 259 House seats as Broderick unseats DesJarlais
stories.summary: Democrat Victoria Broderick defeated eight-term Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee's 4th District, the AP reported Tuesday. The result gives Democrats at least 259 House seats, their largest majority since 1990.
stories.why_it_matters: A majority that large gives Democrats firm control of the House agenda, including spending bills and investigations of the administration, when the new Congress starts in January.
stories.background: Democrats won the House in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, and the size of their majority has grown as close races were settled. Tennessee's 4th District was redrawn by Republicans to take in part of Nashville, and DesJarlais, in office since 2011, had beaten Broderick by a wide margin in 2024. Local outlets reported the final margin was about 280 votes and that DesJarlais conceded on Nov. 16 after provisional ballots were counted.

facts.text: Democrat Victoria Broderick won Tennessee's 4th Congressional District, narrowly defeating Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais.
The win gave Democrats at least 259 House seats, the largest majority since 1990.
Broderick, a tech support worker, won without airing a single TV ad, The New York Times reported.
The margin was about 280 votes, and DesJarlais conceded on Nov. 16 after provisional ballots were counted.
Republican redistricting moved part of Nashville into the district, where Broderick ran up a large lead.

stories.headline: Unsealed records show judge first resisted search of Rep. Ilhan Omar's home
stories.summary: A federal court released heavily redacted records about last month's FBI search of Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington home. They show a magistrate judge first raised constitutional concerns about searching a sitting member of Congress, and that the warrant sought evidence going back to 1980. The New York Post reported that a grand jury has been empaneled in the case.
stories.why_it_matters: A search of a sitting lawmaker's home is rare and raises questions about the limits on executive power over Congress. No charges have been filed, and the case could lead to an indictment of a member of Congress.
stories.background: Federal agents searched Omar's D.C. home on Oct. 12 as part of an investigation that reports describe as focused on possible immigration-related fraud. Omar, a Minnesota Democrat, has not been charged and denies wrongdoing. News organizations and the group Judicial Watch asked the court to unseal the warrant, and Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered a partial, redacted release while keeping most of the affidavit sealed.

facts.text: A federal court on Monday released heavily redacted documents about the October search of Omar's D.C. home.
Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh warned the Justice Department that its warrant could violate the Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause, and initially blocked the search.
The magistrate judge ruled that Omar was entitled to assert privacy protections that apply to sitting members of Congress at the outset of the search.
The warrant application covers a period starting in 1980, and no criminal charges are listed in the records.
Prosecutors say they are pursuing evidence of crimes allegedly committed over decades and unrelated to her work in Congress.
Justice Department lawyers argued that Judge James Boasberg's decision to unseal the records contradicts his own ruling in a Trump case.
The New York Post reported that a federal grand jury has been empaneled in the case; it is unclear what charges are being sought.
Omar has not been charged and denies wrongdoing.

stories.headline: Hackers breach unclassified CIA and ODNI systems
stories.summary: An unclassified CIA system used to analyze open-source intelligence was breached in a cyberattack, according to people familiar with the incident who spoke to several outlets. Reporting also says the Office of the Director of National Intelligence was affected. An official said there was no disruption to critical capabilities.
stories.why_it_matters: It is the latest in a run of attacks on federal agencies and companies, raising questions about how well government networks that hold data on Americans are protected.
stories.background: The CIA and ODNI run both classified networks and separate unclassified systems used for routine work and public-source research. Breaches of unclassified government systems are more common, but they can still expose sensitive details about how agencies work. The incident follows several weeks of cyberattacks and tech outages affecting U.S. government departments and major companies. Officials have not publicly named who was behind it.

facts.text: An unclassified CIA system was breached in a cyberattack; the breach did not involve classified information and the issue has been resolved, a person familiar with it told the AP.
The CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence suffered a breach of some unclassified information, according to The New York Times and a Reuters source.
Information at other government agencies was also believed to have been exposed, and it was not clear exactly what material was compromised.
Fox News sources said the affected network is used to analyze open-source intelligence and that the FBI is involved.
An official said the breach caused no disruption to critical capabilities.
The breach follows a series of cyberattacks on U.S. government departments and major companies in recent weeks.

stories.headline: Trump awards Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom
stories.summary: President Trump gave Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor, in the Oval Office on Tuesday. Giuliani led New York City through the 9/11 attacks and later, as Trump's personal lawyer, was central to efforts to overturn the 2020 election.
stories.why_it_matters: The award shows how the president is using the country's top civilian honor, and it revives debate over the 2020 election fight in which Giuliani played a leading role.
stories.background: Giuliani was New York's mayor from 1994 to 2001 and was widely praised for his leadership after the Sept. 11 attacks, earning the nickname "America's mayor." He ran for the Republican presidential nomination in 2008 and later became Trump's personal lawyer. After he pushed false claims of fraud in the 2020 election, he was disbarred, and a jury ordered him to pay large damages to two Georgia election workers he defamed.

stories.headline: Houthis strike Riyadh financial tower again and claim attack on Saudi refinery
stories.summary: Yemen's Houthis said they attacked the tower housing Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund in Riyadh and the Ras Tanura oil refinery, calling it retaliation for strikes on their territory. Eleven people were reported injured at the tower, the second attack on it in under a week. The group also threatened Saudi Red Sea ports, including Jeddah, while its fighters press toward the Yemeni government's seat in Aden.
stories.why_it_matters: Attacks on Saudi oil sites and its financial hub add risk to global oil supplies, which can show up in fuel prices, and the fighting around Aden threatens a wider humanitarian crisis in Yemen.
stories.background: The Houthis are an Iran-backed armed movement that has controlled Yemen's capital and much of the north for about a decade, fighting a Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Their attacks on Saudi Arabia resumed this autumn alongside a wider regional war involving Iran and the United States. Strikes have hit Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District several times this month, including an earlier hit on the same tower on Nov. 19 that damaged several floors without injuries. On the ground in Yemen, the Houthis have taken much of the western coastline and are advancing on Aden, the government's temporary capital.

facts.text: The Houthis claimed attacks on Riyadh's financial district and the Ras Tanura refinery in eastern Saudi Arabia, describing them as retaliation for strikes on Houthi-held territory.
Eleven people were injured in the attack on the Public Investment Fund tower, the second strike on the building in six days; the earlier one caused no casualties.
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence described the strike on the tower as a "terrorist attack"; at least two Indian nationals were among the injured and India's government condemned it.
A fire was reported at the Ras Tanura refinery, according to Deutsche Welle.
The Houthis said Jeddah and all other Saudi Red Sea ports would be targeted if Saudi Arabia attacks the Yemeni port of Hodeidah.
Houthi forces have advanced close to Aden, where Yemeni government troops are holding a fortified line; government forces said the Houthis will not take the city.
The Nov. 19 strike on the same tower damaged several floors and caused no injuries, and Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry said it reserved the right to take all necessary measures in response.

stories.headline: Solomon Islands signs security treaty with Australia, barring foreign bases
stories.summary: The Solomon Islands signed a treaty naming Australia its primary security partner and stating that no foreign military or security base will be allowed on its territory. Several outlets reported that it sets aside the country's 2022 security pact with China, which had raised concern about a possible Chinese naval presence in the South Pacific.
stories.why_it_matters: The deal shifts a contest between China and the U.S. and its allies over Pacific islands that sit along key shipping and military routes. Right-leaning outlets in the ingest covered it mainly through the Telegraph's paywalled piece on China's setback.
stories.background: The Solomon Islands is a nation of about 700,000 people roughly 2,000 kilometers northeast of Australia. In 2022 its then government signed a secretive security agreement with China, alarming Australia and the U.S., which feared it could open the way for a Chinese military base. Prime Minister Matthew Wale, who took office this year, said in June he would review the China pact and agreed with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to negotiate a broad treaty covering security and the economy. This week's signing is the result.

facts.text: The treaty names Australia the Solomon Islands' "primary security partner."
The treaty states there will be no foreign military or security base in the Solomon Islands.
The Solomon Islands is setting aside its 2022 security agreement with China, according to the BBC and the AP.
Prime Minister Matthew Wale said his country would no longer be a point of regional uncertainty, the BBC reported.
Under the pact, the Solomon Islands will reject any foreign power trying to interfere with its sensitive infrastructure, Deutsche Welle reported.
In June, Wale announced a review of the China pact and agreed with Albanese to negotiate a comprehensive treaty with Australia.

stories.headline: China opens investigation into Shanghai party chief Chen Jining
stories.summary: China's Communist Party placed Chen Jining, Shanghai's party secretary and a member of the 24-member Politburo, under investigation for suspected serious violations of party discipline and law, state media said. He is the fourth Politburo member to be investigated since 2025.

stories.background: Since taking power in 2012, Xi Jinping has run an anti-corruption campaign that has removed officials from local cadres to generals and members of the top leadership. Investigations announced as "violations of party discipline" usually precede expulsion and prosecution. Chen Jining, a former environmental engineer and president of Tsinghua University, became Shanghai's party chief in 2022 after serving as Beijing's mayor. The party is due to pick a new leadership lineup at its congress in 2027.

stories.summary: A federal jury in New York found Chinese telecom company Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, after a three-month trial. stories.background: Huawei is one of the world's largest makers of telecom equipment and smartphones. U.S. prosecutors in Brooklyn charged the company in 2019 and later added racketeering counts, accusing it of a long-running scheme to take technology from U.S. firms and of hiding business in Iran from banks. The case led to the 2018 arrest in Canada of Huawei's finance chief, Meng Wanzhou, who returned to China in 2021 under a deal with prosecutors. Huawei has denied wrongdoing throughout.

stories.headline: Colombian forces end Cartagena supermarket hostage siege
stories.summary: Colombian police and soldiers stormed a supermarket in Cartagena early Wednesday, ending a day-long siege by armed men who took shoppers and staff hostage after a failed attempt to rob an armored truck. President Abelardo de la Espriella said all hostages were rescued and one captor was killed.

President Abelardo de la Espriella, a right-wing leader, has carried out a broad crackdown on the drug trade. On Monday a car bomb outside regional government offices in the central city of Villavicencio injured 23 people. The Cartagena siege began Tuesday when an armored-truck robbery failed and the gunmen fled into a supermarket.

stories.summary: Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi and members of her production team each received 74 lashes over an online concert in which she sang without the mandatory head covering, according to her lawyers and local media. stories.background: Iranian law requires women to cover their hair in public, and women are barred from singing solo in public. stories.headline: South African court sets aside Phala Phala report against Ramaphosa
stories.summary: South Africa's Western Cape High Court set aside in full the independent panel report that found President Cyril Ramaphosa had a case to answer over the 2020 theft of U.S. dollars from his Phala Phala farm. A parliamentary panel set up under Section 89 of the constitution found in 2022 that he may have a case to answer, but Parliament voted not to proceed. In May 2026 the Constitutional Court ruled that vote unconstitutional, and Ramaphosa went to the Western Cape High Court to have the panel report set aside, winning an interim halt to the impeachment inquiry in July.

stories.headline: AI stocks pull Wall Street back down as the Huang relief rally fades
stories.summary: U.S. stocks gave back part of Monday's big rally on Tuesday as Nvidia, Anthropic and other artificial intelligence stocks fell, according to the Associated Press and The Wall Street Journal. Nasdaq futures dropped more than 2% early Wednesday, and investors are waiting on October inflation data and a revised estimate of third-quarter economic growth.
stories.why_it_matters: AI companies make up a large share of the indexes that most 401(k)s and index funds track, so these swings show up in people's retirement savings. Wednesday's inflation report could shape whether the Federal Reserve keeps borrowing costs high.
stories.background: Stocks tied to artificial intelligence have swung sharply this month. Nvidia, the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom, lost its chief executive, Jensen Huang, on Nov. 12 amid a personal scandal, and AI stocks sold off hard late last week. When Nvidia reinstated Huang, the Nasdaq Composite jumped 6.5% on Monday. Anthropic, the AI developer that went public on Nov. 19 in the largest IPO on record, has been falling at the same time.

facts.text: The Nasdaq Composite closed 6.5% higher on Monday after Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's CEO, erasing its losses from Friday, CBS News reported.

U.S. stocks finished mixed on Tuesday, with the Nasdaq and S&P 500 giving back some of Monday's gains as traders weighed President Trump's push to reinstall Huang, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Nvidia shares fell Tuesday as investors refocused on the political and governance risks around Huang's reinstatement, France 24 reported.
Nasdaq futures slid more than 2% early Wednesday, according to Reuters and The Wall Street Journal.

Treasury and European government bond yields fell Wednesday morning as investors awaited October personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation data and the second estimate of third-quarter GDP, the Journal reported.

Some strategists remain upbeat: JPMorgan said the S&P 500 is headed to 8,200, and Deutsche Bank's Binky Chadha forecast a rally to 9,000 by the end of next year. Reuters reported that signals in the options market suggest waiting before buying the dip.

stories.summary: President Trump is preparing a new round of tariffs on China, the European Union, Mexico, Japan and about a dozen other trading partners, the New York Post and Fox Business reported, citing a report. China responded Wednesday that the prospect was 'political maneuvering' and said the two countries should work to keep their trade truce, according to Bloomberg.
stories.why_it_matters: New tariffs would raise the cost of imported goods, which tends to reach shoppers through higher prices. Reports of the U.S. plan in today's coverage come mainly from right-leaning outlets, while the Chinese response was reported by Bloomberg.
stories.background: Tariffs are taxes on imported goods, paid by the importing company and often passed on to customers. The Trump administration has imposed several rounds of tariffs during his second term, including duties of 10% and 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners earlier this year. The U.S. and China have been operating under a trade truce that eased tensions between the world's two largest economies. Markets have been sensitive to any sign that the truce could break down.

stories.headline: Huang apologizes to Nvidia staff as U.S. blacklists chip firm tied to the scandal
stories.summary: Reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees on Tuesday and acknowledged violating the company's code of conduct, while denying that President Trump was instrumental in his return, The Guardian reported. The Commerce Department added Singapore-based Megaspeed, a company at the center of the scandal, to its trade blacklist, and Reuters reported that firms linked to Alice Huang listed $270 million in AI servers in China.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is one of the largest companies in the stock market and the main supplier of AI chips, so questions about its leadership and about chips reaching China affect both investors and U.S. export policy.
stories.background: Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia and ran it for three decades before resigning on Nov. 12 after reports of extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman. U.S. investigators have been examining whether Megaspeed, a Nvidia customer, diverted restricted chips to China, and the Justice Department is leading a criminal probe. Nvidia reinstated Huang this week after Trump publicly backed his return, a move that drew criticism from lawmakers in both parties and from U.S. allies. Officials had disagreed for weeks over whether to blacklist Megaspeed.

facts.text: Huang apologized to staff on Tuesday, said he had made 'terrible mistakes' and acknowledged violating the code of conduct by having extramarital affairs, The Guardian reported; Reuters, citing a source, also reported that he said he violated the code.
The administration added Megaspeed to the entity list, a trade blacklist, after weeks of disagreement among top officials, The New York Times reported.
Companies linked to Alice Huang raised financing against AI computing equipment for data centers in China, listing $270 million in servers, according to records reviewed by Reuters.
A German government minister said he was 'shocked' by Trump's intervention on Nvidia, Reuters reported.
Rep. Greg Steube, a Florida Republican, called Trump's intervention unprecedented in an interview with Fox Business.
The Justice Department is leading a criminal investigation into Megaspeed over possible violations of U.S. chip export controls.

stories.headline: Microsoft declares 'Code Red' after its Nov. 12-13 outage, Reuters reports
stories.summary: Microsoft has declared an internal 'Code Red' after the Nov. 12-13 outage that took down Teams, Outlook, Copilot and other services, according to internal memos seen by Reuters. Chief executive Satya Nadella blamed an undetected Windows defect introduced in July, the New York Post reported.
stories.why_it_matters: Many workplaces, schools and governments depend on Microsoft's email and collaboration tools, so a 24-hour failure halts ordinary work. In today's ingest the story was carried by Reuters and right-leaning outlets, with no left-leaning outlet coverage.
stories.background: Microsoft runs widely used cloud services, including Outlook email, Teams and its Copilot AI assistant. On Nov. 12 and 13 those services went down for about a day for many users worldwide. Microsoft later said the cause was a software defect it introduced in July that lay dormant until load surged on its network gateway servers. Nadella apologized publicly and said the problem should have been caught in testing.

stories.headline: Amazon warns customers a Council delivery bill could add up to $5 per order
stories.summary: Amazon is showing New York City customers pop-up warnings that a City Council bill, the Delivery Protection Act, 'could add up to $5 per order,' and urging them to contact their Council members. The bill, backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, would license last-mile delivery hubs and require companies to employ drivers directly rather than through contractors. Separately, THE CITY reported that the state Labor Department is investigating Amazon's JFK8 warehouse on Staten Island.
stories.why_it_matters: New Yorkers who shop online are being asked to weigh in on a bill that could change how packages reach their doors and how delivery drivers are employed; the $5 figure is Amazon's own estimate, not a charge in the bill. Coverage in the digest comes from center and lean-left outlets only.
stories.background: Amazon delivers most packages in the city through independent 'delivery service partners' whose drivers are not Amazon employees. Intro 518, sponsored by Council Member Tiffany Cabán, would require owners of certain last-mile delivery facilities to get a city license and directly employ the workers, which supporters say would improve pay and safety and make it easier to unionize. A version of the bill stalled in 2025; Mayor Mamdani has since backed it. Amazon and a coalition of logistics firms say it would raise costs and threaten jobs.

facts.text: Amazon is showing NYC customers a notice saying the Council 'could add up to $5 per order' and urging them to contact Council members.
The bill would require owners of certain last-mile delivery facilities to be licensed by the city's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection and to employ delivery workers directly.
The bill itself does not impose a per-order surcharge; Amazon says its requirements would raise delivery costs, and the New York Times reported the $5 claim is 'more complicated.'
Mayor Zohran Mamdani supports the bill.

stories.headline: State's top court rules landlords cannot turn away tenants who use housing vouchers
stories.summary: New York's Court of Appeals ruled 4-3 on Monday that landlords cannot refuse to rent to people paying with government housing assistance, amNY reported. The decision overturns a lower appellate ruling that had struck down the state's source-of-income protections, rejecting upstate landlords' argument that required inspections made the law unconstitutional.
stories.why_it_matters: Tens of thousands of New Yorkers rent with Section 8 or city vouchers; the ruling restores the state law that bars landlords from rejecting them for how they pay. This was reported by amNY alone in the digest.
stories.background: A 2019 state law made it illegal to discriminate against renters based on lawful source of income, including housing vouchers; New York City has had its own similar law since 2008. Upstate landlords challenged the state law, arguing that voucher programs require inspections of their units, which they said violated their Fourth Amendment rights. In March 2026 the Appellate Division's Third Department agreed and found the law unconstitutional, and the state attorney general appealed. Monday's decision from the Court of Appeals, the state's highest court, reverses that ruling.

facts.text: The Court of Appeals ruled 4-3 on Monday that landlords cannot refuse to rent to people using government housing assistance.
The decision overturned a lower appellate court ruling, rejecting upstate landlords' argument centered on voucher inspection requirements.

stories.headline: MTA withholds payments from OMNY contractor Cubic over troubled rollout
stories.summary: The MTA is holding back 'millions and millions' of dollars from Cubic Transportation Systems, the company building the OMNY tap-to-pay fare system, THE CITY reported. The transit agency is seeking money over delays and problems in the rollout of the MetroCard's replacement.
stories.why_it_matters: OMNY is how most subway and bus riders now pay, and the dispute is over public money spent on a system that has run years late. Only THE CITY reported this in the digest.
stories.background: The MTA awarded Cubic a $573 million contract in 2017 to replace the MetroCard with OMNY, which lets riders tap a phone, bank card or OMNY card. The contract's cost later grew to about $772 million, and the rollout has been marked by delays, software problems that caused mistaken charges, and the MTA moving some work away from Cubic in 2024. The MetroCard is being phased out.

stories.headline: City report says more frequent cab fare increases could help drivers stay out of poverty
stories.summary: A new Taxi and Limousine Commission report found that the cost of owning and operating a taxi or for-hire vehicle has risen about 16% on average since the city last raised cab fares in 2022. The report says more frequent fare increases could help keep drivers out of poverty.
stories.why_it_matters: The report could set up higher yellow-cab fares for riders, while drivers say rising costs are squeezing their incomes.
stories.background: The TLC sets yellow-cab fares and minimum pay for app-based drivers. It has approved only one fare increase for yellow cabs in the past 14 years, in late 2022, which raised fares by roughly 23% on average. Drivers, many still dealing with the fallout of the medallion debt crisis, have pushed for regular adjustments as insurance, fuel and vehicle costs rise.

stories.headline: Trump calls congestion pricing 'a killer' and vows to keep it out of other cities
stories.summary: President Trump said Manhattan's congestion pricing toll is 'a killer' for New York and said he would not allow it in any other metropolitan area, the New York Post reported. He did not announce a new step against the New York toll in the report.
stories.why_it_matters: Drivers entering lower Manhattan pay the toll, and it funds MTA upgrades, so continued federal hostility keeps its future in question. Only the right-leaning New York Post covered this in the digest.
stories.background: New York began charging most vehicles to enter Manhattan below 60th Street in January 2025, with the money going to MTA capital projects. The Trump administration moved to revoke federal approval of the program in February 2025, and New York sued; a federal judge blocked the administration from cutting off funding while the case continues. Gov. Kathy Hochul and the MTA have kept the tolls running.

stories.headline: Design panel to vote Monday on $8 billion casino near Citi Field
stories.summary: The city's Public Design Commission is set to vote Monday on the design of the $8 billion Hard Rock Hotel and Casino at Metropolitan Park next to Citi Field, Gothamist reported. Commissioners delayed a vote last month over questions about how the complex would manage stormwater.
stories.why_it_matters: The casino, backed by Mets owner Steve Cohen, would reshape a stretch of Flushing Meadows that floods, and Monday's vote is one of its remaining city approvals. Only Gothamist covered it in the digest.
stories.background: Metropolitan Park is a casino, hotel and entertainment complex planned on parking lots beside Citi Field by Mets owner Steve Cohen and Hard Rock. The state Gaming Commission approved it as one of three downstate casino licenses in December 2025. The Public Design Commission reviews the parts of the project facing public parkland, and last month it postponed a vote, asking for more detail on stormwater management, gates and glass. Opponents have raised flooding concerns.

concept.explanation: The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index measures how much the prices of the things Americans buy are changing, from groceries to rent to medical care. It is the inflation gauge the Federal Reserve watches most closely, and the October reading is due this week. A hotter-than-expected number makes the Fed less likely to cut interest rates, which keeps mortgage, car-loan and credit-card rates high; a cooler one raises the odds that borrowing gets cheaper. It moves with energy prices, wages, housing costs and anything else that changes what households pay, including tariffs on imported goods.
